Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

extra adjective and adverb

more than the usual or the needed number

also additional, an extra, one more, two more, added on

classical

Verg. A. 11.285: sī duo praetereā tālīs …, glossed “two more” by Lewis & Short
Caes. B.G. 4.22: quicquid praetereā nāvium habēbat (Lewis & Short)

praetereā

adverb, beside the noun or the number

besides, in addition: one more, two more

Latin has no adjective for “extra”: it names the thing and adds praetereā, “besides”, or puts amplius with a number (see further). The same adverb opens an added point, “moreover”.

Other words

  • accessiō, accessiōnis f. — an extra, an addition; something added on

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.138: hanc Scaurus dēmōlītus accessiōnem adjūnxit aedibus, Scaurus pulled the house down and built on an extension; Cic. Lael. 11: quid igitur hunc paucōrum annōrum accessiō juvāre potuisset?

    The noun for the thing added to something larger: an extension to a house, a few extra years, a thing thrown in. Its first sense is an approach, a coming near; in medicine it is the onset of a fever (Lewis & Short).

  • supervacāneus, supervacānea, supervacāneum — spare, extra: more than is needed

    adjective · also used · classical · Cato Agr. 12: vāsa supervacānea, glossed “supernumerary, extra” by Lewis & Short; Cic. N.D. 2.121: ut nihil eōrum supervacāneum sit (Lewis & Short)

    Its usual sense is needless, superfluous (Cicero, Sallust, Livy), so it suits a spare thing kept beyond what is needed, and can sound like a reproach: “one too many”.

Examples

  • sī duo praetereā tālīs Īdaea tulisset terra virōs …

    if the land of Ida had borne two more such men …Verg. A. 11.285–286

  • Cape lōdīcem praetereā ūnam, sī algēs.

    Take an extra blanket if you’re cold.composed

See also further, more, else.
